title: Profit Block
statement: A shop recorded its daily profit in profits (a negative number is a loss). The owner must report one block of consecutive days whose length is at least minLen and at most maxLen. Return the largest total profit that a valid block can have. A block has to be reported even if every valid block loses money.

examples.explanation: The days [5, -4, -1, 6] total 6, and so do the days [3, -2, 5]. No other block of 2 to 4 days does better (for example [6, -3, 2] totals 5), so the answer is 6.
Every valid block loses money. The best one is [-4, -2] with a total of -6; the whole record totals -13.

hints.content: A block's total is the difference between two running totals of the record. If the end of the block is fixed, what do you want to know about the possible starts?
For a fixed end the valid starts form a window of positions, and when the end moves right the whole window moves right by one. You want the smallest running total inside that window.
Looking at every start in the window for every end is up to about 200 million steps at 20,000 days. You need a structure that reports the window minimum cheaply as the window slides.

Keep a deque of candidate start positions whose running totals increase from front to back. A new start removes every back entry whose running total is at least as large, because the new start is later and no worse.

Drop front entries that have fallen out of the window (too far from the end). The front is then the best start, giving prefix[end] - prefix[front]. Each position enters and leaves the deque once: O(n). Use an index-based deque, since array.shift() is O(n).

testCases.explanation: A mixed record where two blocks tie for the best.
Only losses: the answer is the least bad block.
Any block length is allowed, so the best block is just the single day of 9.
A long minimum length forces a block that contains one or both of the profitable days.
A random medium record with a window of 34 allowed lengths.
The largest record with every length allowed: about 200 million blocks for a brute-force check.
The largest record with lengths between 7,000 and 13,000, about 120 million block checks for brute force.
The largest record alternating between -9 and 9, with tied prefix totals everywhere.

solutions.title: Extend every block from every start
solutions.intuition: Try each start and grow the block one day at a time, tracking the running sum.
solutions.approach: For each start, add days one by one up to maxLen. Whenever the length is at least minLen, compare the sum with the best.
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n * maxLen), up to about 200 million additions at n = 20,000
commonMistakes: Starting best at 0, which is wrong when every block loses money.
Checking length >= minLen only for the final length of each start.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Growing each block incrementally avoids recomputing sums but still visits every start and every allowed length. At 20,000 days with a wide length range that is hundreds of millions of steps, so the window minimum must be maintained instead.

steps.title: Starting at day 0
steps.content: For [3, -2, 5, -4, -1, 6, -3, 2] with lengths 2 to 4, start 0 gives totals 1, 6 and 2 for lengths 2, 3 and 4.

steps.title: Other starts
steps.content: Start 2 gives 1, 0 and 6 for lengths 2, 3 and 4, so the best over all starts is 6.

solutions.title: Prefix sums with a range-minimum table
solutions.intuition: A block total is prefix[end] minus prefix[start], so for each end the best start is the minimum prefix in a range; a sparse table answers any range minimum in O(1) after O(n log n) setup.
solutions.approach: Build prefix totals. Build a sparse table whose level k stores the minimum of 2^k consecutive prefix values. For each end from minLen to n, take the minimum prefix over starts max(0, end - maxLen) to end - minLen using two overlapping power-of-two ranges, and update the best of prefix[end] - that minimum.
solutions.pseudocode:
prefix[0..n]; table[0] = prefix; table[k][i] = min(table[k-1][i], table[k-1][i + 2^(k-1)])
for end in minLen..n: low = max(0, end - maxLen); high = end - minLen
  k = floor(log2(high - low + 1)); m = min(table[k][low], table[k][high - 2^k + 1])
  best = max(best, prefix[end] - m)
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n log n) to build and O(n) queries
solutions.spaceComplexity: O(n log n): about 15 arrays of 20,001 entries
commonMistakes: Using two ranges that do not overlap correctly: the second starts at high - 2^k + 1, not low + 2^k.
Building levels with the wrong length so a query reads past the end of the table.
solutions.interviewExplanation: The window minimum is a static range-minimum query on the prefix array, and a sparse table answers it with two lookups. It costs O(n log n) memory, so the deque, which is O(n) time and O(n) memory, is preferable, but this version is easier to reason about.

steps.title: Build
steps.content: The prefix array is [0, 3, 1, 6, 2, 1, 7, 4, 6]; level 1 holds minima of pairs and level 2 minima of four.

steps.title: Query
steps.content: For end 3, starts 0 to 1 give minimum 0, so the total is 6 - 0 = 6; the best over all ends stays 6.

solutions.title: Prefix sums with a monotonic deque
solutions.intuition: As the end moves right, the allowed starts slide right too, so the minimum prefix in the window can be kept in a deque that discards dominated candidates.
solutions.approach: Build prefix totals. For each end from minLen to n, push the newly allowed start end - minLen after popping every back entry whose prefix is at least as large, pop the front while it is older than end - maxLen, and compare prefix[end] - prefix[front] with the best.
solutions.pseudocode:
deque of start indices, prefix increasing front to back
for end in minLen..n: s = end - minLen
  while deque not empty and prefix[back] >= prefix[s]: pop back
  push s
  while front < end - maxLen: pop front
  best = max(best, prefix[end] - prefix[front])
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n): each start is pushed and popped at most once
solutions.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the prefix array and the deque
commonMistakes: Leaving entries older than end - maxLen at the front, so a stale minimum is used.
Pushing the start before checking that it is at least minLen days old.
Using array.shift() for the front, which makes the loop quadratic.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Each end wants the smallest prefix total among starts in [end - maxLen, end - minLen]. That window moves one step right per end, so this is a sliding-window minimum over the prefix array, which a monotonic deque solves in amortized O(1). A start that is both later and no smaller than an earlier one will outlive it in the window and never lose to it, so the earlier one can be dropped. An index-based deque in a typed array avoids shift costs.

steps.title: Prefix totals
steps.content: For the first example the prefix totals are 0, 3, 1, 6, 2, 1, 7, 4, 6.

steps.title: Slide the window
steps.content: At end 3 the allowed starts are 0 to 1 and the cheapest prefix is 0, giving 6; at end 7 the starts are 3 to 5 with minimum 1, giving 4 - 1 = 3, and so on. The best stays 6.
